title: Ivy and the Sunstone Fluff
markdown:
The High Valley Archipelago kept its peaks in the clouds’ appointment book. Rope ferries groaned between them like clocks that had never learned punctuality, and bells stitched silver through the mist until the air itself seemed to hum with leftover tunes. In a cottage that had lost a polite argument with clutter lived Ivy, a witch whose magic hummed like well-wound clockwork. She mended more than she conjured. She was not the wart-and-cackle variety. Practicality was the eccentricity: ingredients sat by scent rather than colour, sunshine-dried rosemary beside moon-bathed lavender, and she stitched torn cloud-fluff with a whisper-light thread that made the sky look, if you were fussy, a fraction tidier.

Coal was essential, and Ivy used the word without irony. The raven’s feathers drank light and left a private shadow even at noon. Intelligence sat in the obsidian of his eyes and missed nothing: not a squirrel’s twitch, not a dewdrop on silk. He did not merely caw. Remarks arrived with a head-tilt, usually concerning other people’s inefficiency or the exact bush that was hiding a ripe berry.

A package arrived on a blustery afternoon, wrapped in rough twine and smelling faintly of a travelling merchant’s lost socks and, if you were unlucky, disgruntled llama. Curiosity, which Ivy treated as a tool rather than a vice, undid the knot with a flick. Inside, on a bed of dried mountain lavender, lay the Sunstone. Not a pebble. The heart of the valley, the legendary insurance of prosperity, the warmth of the annual Solstice Fair. Legend claimed its glow ran on shared joy. When she turned it in her hands, unease went down her spine without consulting the wind outside. The Sunstone was dimming. Not a collapse, not theatre. A slow, almost rude fade, the sort you notice only after you have been looking.

“That is not good,” Coal said, brow-feathers in conference. “The mist looks more permanent than usual.”

News ran faster than a runaway sheep with a slope to spend. The bell-ringers, whose fingers were usually steady, worried their chimes would go cold and lose the cheerful ring. The ferry-men, calloused from years of rope, fretted about brittleness mid-crossing. And then there was Wizard Thaddeus Flickerwick.

Ah, Thaddeus. His tower, on the highest, most showy peak, pulsed with light and glitter, a magnificent and slightly alarming confection of polished crystal and gold leaf. Flowing robes the colour of sunsets. Dramatic pronouncements. Hair in gravity-defying spikes that glinted as if gravity had been given notice. He arrived in a shower of golden sparks that made even Coal sneeze, voice booming like a playful thunderstorm.

“Fear not, good people. Wizard Thaddeus is here to reignite celestial radiance. Prepare for a spectacle of cosmic proportions.” He struck a pose that threatened a career in thistles, and produced a wand that looked suspiciously like a polished peacock feather, complete with iridescent eye-spots.

Ivy, from a crooked doorway, apron in spell-dust, lifted one eyebrow. “If you are going to be mysterious, Thaddeus, you could at least be punctual. The Fair is rather important.”

He huffed glitter. “The universe does not run on clockwork. This requires drama. Your tinkering mends teacups. It does not make legend.”

Ivy preferred observation to legend. Over-the-top magic, in her experience, was often a curtain for not having looked. She and Coal took the mist-laden slopes. They spoke with a baker whose loaves had gone pale, as if they had seen a ghost and taken it personally. They listened to a goat-herder who grumbled about wool prices and the general incompetence of kids, meaning the four-legged kind. Then, as the mist thickened and considered swallowing them whole, they found Jocelyn Button-Nose.

Jocelyn was an ogre shepherd, the sort people invent as lumbering and dim, prone to tripping over feet the size of luggage. She was large, yes, and her nose was indeed a perfectly formed smooth brown button, which gave her a perpetually questioning look. Dim, she was not. She sat on a mossy outcrop while enormous shaggy sheep, wool the colour of storm-cloud, grazed as if they had been briefed. Profound calm lived on her face. She seemed to have absorbed the landscape until moss and rock had a say in her posture.

“Master Button-Nose?” Ivy said, because courtesy costs nothing and ogres notice.

Jocelyn’s earth-brown eyes found her. The smile was slow. “Aye.” Thunder, but sitting down.

“The Sunstone,” Coal croaked, then remembered manners. “It is not shining as it did.”

Jocelyn nodded, and the ground considered nodding back. “Ah. Quite mossy, isn’t it?”

Ivy looked at Coal. Mossy was not in Thaddeus’s pamphlet. Her quiet magic, for a blink, wondered if it was enough. The peacock wand, in the damp, had already begun to sulk. This problem, at least, had texture.

“A particular moss,” Jocelyn said, pointing with a thick, careful finger. “Grown for celebration. And a bit of artistic expression.”

The Fluff-Whisperer Herd, she explained, were not ordinary goats. Their wool was the colour of twilight and softer than a sigh, rumoured to be spun from moonlight and the sort of dreams that refuse to be useful. This year the flamboyant mountain chamois, with horns designed by committee, had stolen the admiration. The goats wanted a trophy that shone and declared fleece-superiority to anyone with eyes. They had cultivated a rare iridescent moss — vibrant green, flecked with amethyst and sapphire — and draped it over the Sunstone as a fluffy, luminous medal, a testament to taste.

“They did not understand it would dim the valley’s light,” Jocelyn said, shaking a head that moved weather. “They only wanted to be admired. They have such pride in their fluff.”

Ivy’s practicality sat up and put its boots on. No booming. No peacock. An exchange. Coal’s wings took the high air; Ivy knew the most hidden peaks, where moonbeams collected like dewdrops on cobwebs. They gathered shimmering lunar thread, silvery, internally radiant, as soft as the goats’ own twilight wool and significantly less obscuring. Prestigious, even. Goats noticed prestige.

She brought the glowing skeins to Jocelyn. “Excellent taste, those goats. I have something that will make them shine without putting the valley to bed.”

Jocelyn climbed with surprising grace and brokered the swap. The finest of the herd plucked moss as if it were jewellery and wove moonbeam into their coats until they were visible from an embarrassing distance. The moss went to the meadows, where it belonged.

Thaddeus, on a showier slope, was preparing the grandest spell in a life of grand spells, oblivious to negotiations among sheep. The air crackled in a way that suggested jam. His cauldron bubbled with something that smelled of strawberries and burnt sugar. A chorus of marmots stood ready to warble an ode to celestial light, complex, slightly off-key, and very sure of itself. The peacock wand quivered with pent-up everything. He was three utterances of “luminescence” and one bewildered levitated owl from glory when the Sunstone came free.

It pulsed. Warmth chased mist down the valley as if mist had an appointment elsewhere. Pine and damp earth arrived together. Bells chimed with a vigour that made silver remember heat. The rope ferries creaked happy, groaning timbers joining the joke.

Thaddeus lowered the feather. Bewildered amusement, then a grudging, actual smile that dimmed his hair a watt.

“Remarkably undramatic. And effective.” A look at Ivy, the stone, Ivy again. “Your quiet magic has a certain elegance.”

Ivy’s private smile reached her eyes. She did not gift him a proverb. Coal winked, which was proverb enough. The Fair would happen. The goats had a prize. Jocelyn watched her flock settle and mentioned, as if discussing weather, that the herd were already planning moss hats for the ferry-men: camouflage, they said, and also fashion.

Ivy laughed into the bells. Coal ruffled, a pledge to monitor millinery. The valley, for once, glowed because someone had looked at the moss instead of the sky.
characters: Ivy (practical witch who mends cloud-fluff), Coal (a midnight raven with obsidian eyes), Thaddeus Flickerwick (a wizard of peacock-feather drama)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
author: StoryGen Community
